Bohr's atomic model: Part 3 practice, worked solutions

For teachers only. The tutor has the same solutions and is told to guide students with questions rather than give answers. Do not share this file with students.

Data used in every task

These are the same values students see on the data card in the sim.

En=−13.6 eVn2 rn=n2⁢r1,r1=0.0529 nm 1λ=R(1nlow2−1nhigh2)
R=1.097×107 m−1 Ephoton=hcλ,hc=1240 eV·nm 1 eV=1.602×10−19 J

Visible light runs from about 380 nm (violet) to 750 nm (red). Shorter is ultraviolet (UV); longer is infrared (IR).

Task 1. Where does Bohr's model fall short?

Bohr's model from 1913 was a huge success: it explained hydrogen's spectrum, and Bohr won the Nobel Prize in 1922. But it is not the model physicists use today.

  1. Which model is used today? Talk about it, ask your teacher, or find out later.
  2. Name 2–3 things that Bohr's model cannot explain, or gets wrong.

a) The model used today

Quantum mechanics, developed by Heisenberg and Schrödinger in 1925–26. The electron does not move in a definite circular orbit. Instead it has a probability cloud (an orbital) that tells where it is likely to be found. The energy levels are still there, and they have the same values as in Bohr's model for hydrogen.

Students do not need to know this from memory. It is fine if they ask the teacher or look it up.

b) What Bohr's model cannot explain (any 2–3 are a full answer)

  • Atoms with more than one electron. It works for hydrogen (and ions with one electron, like He⁺), but fails already for helium.
  • Chemical bonds and molecules. It cannot explain how atoms bind together.
  • Why only these orbits are allowed. Bohr simply postulated it; the model gives no reason.
  • It contradicts classical physics. A charge moving in a circle should radiate light, lose energy and spiral into the nucleus. Bohr just declared that this does not happen.
  • Sharp orbits are wrong. The uncertainty principle says the electron cannot have both an exact position and an exact path.
  • Details of the spectrum. It cannot explain why some lines are brighter than others, why lines split in a magnetic field (the Zeeman effect), or the fine structure (lines that are really two close lines).
What survived: stationary states (fixed energy levels) and quantum jumps with a photon of energy equal to the level difference. Those ideas are exactly what Parts 1 and 2 of the sim are built on.

Task 2. All the ways down

An electron is in orbit 4 of a hydrogen atom. It can get down to orbit 1 in several ways, and it may stop in any orbit on the way.

  1. How many different photons (different wavelengths) can come out in total?
  2. Calculate the wavelength of each one. Which of them can we see?

a) Count the photons

Step 1. List the possible paths from 4 to 1:

  • 4 → 1
  • 4 → 2 → 1
  • 4 → 3 → 1
  • 4 → 3 → 2 → 1

Step 2. Each single jump gives one photon. Collect all the different jumps that appear in the paths: 4→3, 4→2, 4→1, 3→2, 3→1, 2→1. That is every pair of the four levels:

4×32=6

Answer: 6 different photons.

Common mistake: answering 4 (the number of paths) instead of 6 (the number of different jumps). Another is to forget the 4 → 3 jump.

b) Calculate each wavelength

Method. Use the Rydberg formula with the lower level as nlow. Worked example for 4 → 2:

1λ=1.097×107 m−1×(122−142)=1.097×107×0.1875=2.057×106 m−1 λ=12.057×106 m−1=4.862×10−7 m=486 nm

Alternative method (same result): photon energy = difference of level energies, then λ=hc/E. For 4 → 2:

E=E4−E2=(−0.85)−(−3.40)=2.55 eV,λ=1240 eV·nm2.55 eV=486 nm

All six jumps, done the same way:

Jump1nlow2−1nhigh2Photon energyWavelengthType of light
4 → 31/9 − 1/16 = 0.04860.66 eV1875 nmIR
4 → 21/4 − 1/16 = 0.18752.55 eV486 nmvisible, blue-green
4 → 11 − 1/16 = 0.937512.75 eV97.2 nmUV
3 → 21/4 − 1/9 = 0.13891.89 eV656 nmvisible, red
3 → 11 − 1/9 = 0.888912.09 eV102.6 nmUV
2 → 11 − 1/4 = 0.7510.20 eV121.5 nmUV

Answer: only 486 nm (blue-green) and 656 nm (red) are visible. The jumps to orbit 1 give UV, and 4 → 3 gives IR.

Answers that differ in the last digit (for example 97.3 nm or 121.6 nm) come from rounding in the energy method and are correct.

Task 3. The electron that is almost free

In one particular excited state, it takes only 0.85 eV to pull the electron completely free of the hydrogen atom.

  1. Which orbit is the electron in?
  2. How far is it from the proton, in nm and in r₁?
  3. What is the longest wavelength that light can have and still free the electron? What kind of light is it?

a) Which orbit?

Step 1. A free electron has energy 0. To free it from level n you must add exactly −En, so

13.6 eVn2=0.85 eV

Step 2. Solve for n:

n2=13.60.85=16⇒n=4

Answer: orbit 4.

b) Distance from the proton

r4=42⁢r1=16⁢r1=16×0.0529 nm=0.846 nm

Answer: 16 r₁ ≈ 0.85 nm, sixteen times farther out than in the ground state.

c) Longest wavelength that still frees it

Step 1. Longer wavelength means less energy per photon. The longest wavelength that works is the one whose photon has exactly 0.85 eV.

Step 2.

λ=hcE=1240 eV·nm0.85 eV=1459 nm

With the Rydberg formula and nhigh=∞ (free electron):

1λ=R(142−0)⇒λ=16R=1458 nm

Answer: about 1460 nm, which is infrared. Any longer wavelength has too little energy per photon, however bright the light is.

Common mistake: thinking brighter light of a longer wavelength will do. Brightness means more photons, not more energy per photon.

Task 4. Where do the series end?

All jumps that end in orbit 2 are called the Balmer series. All jumps that end in orbit 1 are called the Lyman series.

  1. Find the shortest wavelength in the Balmer series. Can we see it?
  2. Find the longest wavelength in the Lyman series.
  3. Do the two series overlap? Explain your answer.

a) Shortest Balmer wavelength

Step 1. Shortest wavelength = largest energy = the biggest jump down to 2, which starts from very far out (n→∞, so 1/n2→0).

Step 2.

1λ=R(122−0)=R4⇒λ=41.097×107 m−1=364.6 nm

Answer: 364.6 nm. That is just below 380 nm, so it is UV and we cannot see it.

b) Longest Lyman wavelength

Step 1. Longest wavelength = smallest energy = the smallest jump down to 1, which is 2 → 1.

Step 2.

1λ=R(112−122)=3R4⇒λ=43×1.097×107 m−1=121.5 nm

Answer: 121.5 nm (UV).

c) Do they overlap?

Step 1. Find both ends of each series. The Lyman series' shortest wavelength (∞ → 1) is λ=1/R=91.2 nm; the Balmer series' longest (3 → 2) is 656.3 nm.

SeriesShortestLongest
Lyman (ends in 1)91.2 nm121.5 nm
Balmer (ends in 2)364.6 nm656.3 nm

Step 2. Compare: the longest Lyman line (121.5 nm) is far shorter than the shortest Balmer line (364.6 nm).

Answer: no, they do not overlap. Every jump down to orbit 1 releases at least 10.2 eV (the 2 → 1 gap), while every jump down to orbit 2 releases at most 3.4 eV. The big energy gap between levels 1 and 2 separates the two series.
